teaser: A teenager's face, a bush that spells her name, and a missing third of the picture.
review_notes:
Lorenzo di Credi, Portrait of a Young Woman (Metropolitan Museum, New York): juniper behind the sitter, ring in her hands, and a later inscription on the back naming Ginevra de' Benci; whether it shows her is debated. Check.
Marriage to Luigi Niccolini in January 1474 at age 16: standard account; some scholars link the portrait instead to Bernardo Bembo (in Florence 1475 to 1476 and 1478 to 1480).
Panel cut at the bottom, perhaps by up to a third: estimate varies; the Windsor study of hands is often linked to it but not proven.
Reverse: wreath of laurel and palm around a juniper sprig, motto VIRTUTEM FORMA DECORAT; infrared study found Bembo's motto beneath. Check.
Surviving verse line (“I ask your forgiveness and I am a mountain tiger”): check wording.
Bought in 1967 from the Princely House of Liechtenstein for about 5 million dollars, a record at the time.
Fingerprints in the paint are documented by the National Gallery of Art but are not legible in this image.
Size about 38 x 37 cm.

lesson.text: In a museum in New York hangs a small portrait by Lorenzo di Credi. A pale young woman in dark clothes stands before a spiky bush, holding a ring. It looks like a memory of the picture in front of you, repainted by someone who had it in his head. Credi trained in the same Florentine workshop as Leonardo.

That echo matters because it has something this painting lacks: hands. Leonardo's panel is almost square today, about 38 by 37 cm (15 by 14.5 in), smaller than a sheet of newspaper. It was once taller. At some point the bottom was sawn off, perhaps because of damage, and her arms went with it.

A drawing by Leonardo in the British royal collection at Windsor shows a woman's hands, one resting near her chest. Many scholars think it records what the lost lower part of this portrait looked like.

The sitter is Ginevra de' Benci, daughter of a wealthy Florentine banking family. She was about 16 and probably just married, in 1474. Leonardo was 22, still working under his master Verrocchio. This is his first known portrait, and already he hides a riddle in it.
Her name is written in this picture without a single letter. Tap what you think spells “Ginevra.”

spots.title: The juniper
spots.text: The dark bush with needle-sharp leaves is a juniper, ginepro in Italian. Ginepro, Ginevra: a pun that her friends would catch at once. Juniper was also a symbol of a woman's virtue.

lesson.text: The bush does a second job. It wraps her head in darkness, so her skin seems to give off light. And it lets Leonardo break a rule. Florentine women were normally painted in strict profile, indoors, like faces on coins. Ginevra is outside, turned three-quarters toward us.
This is one of the first Italian portraits to turn a woman toward the viewer and set her in open air. Thirty years later Leonardo used the same idea for the Mona Lisa.

He could try this because of a new material. Most Florentines still painted with tempera, pigment mixed with egg, which dries in minutes. Leonardo used oil, the technique of painters from the Netherlands. Oil stays wet for days, so tones can be blended until no brushmark remains.
Leonardo blended with more than brushes. In the sky near the juniper, museum conservators have found his fingerprints, pressed into the wet paint where he softened it with his hand.

lesson.title: What oil paint allows
lesson.text: Three places where the slow-drying paint shows what it can do.

spots.title: Porcelain skin
spots.text: No line marks the edge of the nose or the hollow of the cheek. Light slides into shadow without a step. Her heavy lids and closed mouth give nothing away.

spots.title: Ringlets
spots.text: Each curl is a tiny spiral with its own highlight, painted hair by hair. Leonardo loved spirals all his life: he drew water whirlpools the same way.

spots.title: Blue distance
spots.text: Trees, still water and two thin spires melt into a blue haze. Distant things look paler and bluer through air. Leonardo is already painting the atmosphere itself.

lesson.text: The haze, the plain brown dress, the unsmiling mouth: people have read sadness into her for centuries. We know little for sure. She wrote poetry, and exactly one line survives: “I ask your forgiveness and I am a mountain tiger.” It suits that face rather well.

The back of the panel is painted too. A sprig of juniper sits inside a wreath of laurel and palm, with a Latin motto meaning “Beauty adorns virtue.” Infrared study found another motto underneath, that of Bernardo Bembo, a Venetian ambassador who admired Ginevra and may have ordered the picture.

The National Gallery of Art bought the portrait from the princes of Liechtenstein in 1967 for about five million dollars, then the highest price ever paid for a painting. It remains the only painting by Leonardo on public view in the Americas.

Go back to Credi's woman with her ring and her hands. She is easier to like and easier to forget. Ginevra, cut off at the chest, gives you only a face and a stare. Would the picture hold you this way if the rest had survived?

quiz.question: Why is the juniper bush behind her?
options: It was her family's coat of arms
Its Italian name, ginepro, plays on “Ginevra”
Leonardo painted her in his own garden
quiz.explanation: Ginepro and Ginevra sound alike, and juniper also stood for virtue.

quiz.question: What is missing from the painting today?
options: The lower part, with her hands
quiz.explanation: The bottom of the panel was cut off at some point.

quiz.question: How were Florentine women usually painted before this?
quiz.explanation: Leonardo broke the habit by turning her three-quarters and placing her outside.

quiz.question: What trace of Leonardo have conservators found in the paint?
options: A sketch of the Mona Lisa
quiz.explanation: He softened wet oil paint with his fingers and left prints in the sky.

quiz.question: Why did oil paint help Leonardo blend tones so smoothly?
quiz.explanation: Oil stays wet for days, unlike egg tempera, which dries in minutes.

facts.text: The back of the panel is painted with a wreath and a motto.
facts.explanation: It shows juniper inside laurel and palm, with a motto meaning “Beauty adorns virtue.”

facts.text: Leonardo painted Ginevra de' Benci late in life, after the Mona Lisa.
facts.explanation: He was about 22; the Mona Lisa came some thirty years later.

facts.text: Several paintings by Leonardo are on public view in American museums.
facts.explanation: This is the only one on public view in the Americas.
